intro: Some sports grew slowly over hundreds of years. Basketball did not. A teacher named James Naismith made it up in one winter, in December 1891. He worked at a YMCA school in Springfield, Massachusetts, where snow kept his class indoors.

The game took its shape from that room. The goals were peach baskets nailed to a balcony rail ten feet up, and they are still ten feet high today. Within a few years the game spread to YMCAs, colleges, women's schools and Illinois high schools.

In this unit you will meet the people who made and shared the game, including Senda Berenson and Edwin Henderson. You will read the first rules and follow how the goal changed. You will put real dates in order, from 1891 to 1977.
bigQuestion: How can one room, one teacher and one sheet of rules start a sport that the whole world plays?

test.why: James Naismith invented basketball at the YMCA Training School in December 1891.

test.q: In which city was basketball first played?
test.why: The first game was played at the YMCA Training School in Springfield, Massachusetts.

test.q: Why did Naismith's class need an indoor game?
choices: It was against the law to play outside
Winter kept them off the frozen fields
test.why: Long New England winters pushed the class inside.
A building worker brought peach baskets, and Naismith nailed them to the balcony rail.

test.q: How high was the balcony rail where the first baskets hung?
test.why: The rail was ten feet high, and the goal is still ten feet high today.

test.q: Which rule was one of Naismith's thirteen rules?
choices: A player cannot run while holding the ball
test.why: The thirteen rules said a player could not run while holding the ball.

test.q: What did The Triangle do on 15 January 1892?
choices: It named the game Naismith Ball
It moved the game to Kansas
test.why: The school newspaper printed the rules, which helped the game spread.

test.q: Why were backboards added in the 1890s?
choices: to stop balcony fans from reaching the ball
test.why: Spectators on the balcony interfered with the ball, so gyms put boards behind the baskets.

test.q: What did Senda Berenson do in 1892?
choices: She brought basketball to women at Smith College
She coached the University of Chicago
test.why: Berenson began teaching basketball to her students at Smith College in 1892.

test.q: How was Berenson's women's game different from Naismith's?
choices: The court was split into three zones
test.why: Berenson split the court into three zones, and each player stayed in hers.

test.q: Why did Edwin Henderson start teams for Black students in Washington, D.C.?
choices: They had asked for peach baskets
Schools were segregated, and many gyms kept Black players out
test.why: Washington's schools were segregated, so Henderson built teams and leagues for Black students.

test.q: What was the score of the 1895 Minnesota college game?
test.why: The Minnesota State School of Agriculture beat Hamline 9 to 3 on 9 February 1895.

test.q: Which order of years is correct?
choices: IHSA founded 1900, first boys champion 1908, first girls champion 1977
first girls champion 1908, IHSA founded 1900, first boys champion 1977
first boys champion 1900, IHSA founded 1908, first girls champion 1977
IHSA founded 1977, first boys champion 1908, first girls champion 1900
test.why: The IHSA began in 1900, crowned its first boys champion in 1908 and its first girls champion in 1977.

test.q: What did Title IX, passed in 1972, do?
choices: It set the basket at ten feet
It banned unfair treatment by sex in schools that get federal money
test.why: Title IX is a 1972 federal law about fair treatment of boys and girls in schools.

test.q: Where did basketball become an Olympic sport, and in what year?
test.why: Basketball joined the Olympic Games in Berlin in 1936, and Naismith was there to watch.

write.prompt: Was basketball made by one person, or by many people and places? Use at least two records from this unit, such as the thirteen rules of 1891, The Triangle of 1892, Berenson's 1901 rule guide or the IHSA's 1908 and 1977 titles. Name each one and its year, and explain what it shows.
tips: Name each record and give its year.
Tell who made it: Naismith, Berenson, Henderson or the IHSA.
Put your dates in time order.
Use unit words such as YMCA, backboard, zone and Title IX.
It is fine to say both one person and many people mattered, if you explain why.
